Tata Sons Ltd. v. Greenpeace International and Another
items.text:
Tata Sons Ltd. v. Greenpeace International and Another - Holding 1: Issue: Can fair comment and criticism using a trademark be injuncted at the interlocutory stage?
Holding: An interim injunction cannot be granted to restrain the use of a trademark in fair comment, parody, or environmental critique unless the plaintiff demonstrates that the defense of fair comment is completely unmerited.

items.title: Tata Sons Ltd. v. Greenpeace International and Another
items.text: Tata Sons Ltd. v. Greenpeace International and Another - Paragraph 38: The right to freedom of speech under Article 19(1)(a) protects fair critique and parody. Trademark rights cannot be weaponized to silence public discourse on environmental issues.

items.title: Tata Sons Ltd. v. Greenpeace International and Another
items.text: Tata Sons Ltd. v. Greenpeace International and Another - Paragraph 42: The court must exercise extreme caution before granting prior restraint on speech. An injunction is declined where fair comment is pleaded with reasonable grounds.

items.title: Tata Sons Ltd. v. Greenpeace International and Another
items.text:
Tata Sons Ltd. v. Greenpeace International and Another - Ratio Decidendi: In defamation and trademark disparagement claims, the Bonnard v. Perryman rule applies: courts will not restrain alleged defamatory matter or parody by interlocutory injunction when the defendant pleads justification or fair comment under Article 19(1)(a).
[Citations: 2011:DHC:452 | 178 (2011) DLT 705]

items.title: Christian Louboutin SAS v. Nakul Bajaj and Others
items.text:
Christian Louboutin SAS v. Nakul Bajaj and Others - Holding 1: Issue: Is an active e-commerce market place entitled to safe harbor under Section 79 IT Act?
Holding: An e-commerce platform that actively assists, promotes, packages, or authenticates goods loses its passive intermediary status and cannot claim exemption from liability under Section 79(1) of the IT Act.

items.title: Christian Louboutin SAS v. Nakul Bajaj and Others
items.text: Christian Louboutin SAS v. Nakul Bajaj and Others - Paragraph 61: Section 79 of the IT Act is not an absolute exemption. If the intermediary's role extends beyond merely providing access or transmission, and involves active promotion, transport, or packaging of counterfeit items, safe harbour is forfeited.

items.title: Christian Louboutin SAS v. Nakul Bajaj and Others
items.text: Christian Louboutin SAS v. Nakul Bajaj and Others - Paragraph 70: The seller cannot hide behind the veil of being a neutral intermediary when it exercises pervasive control over the display, price structuring, and delivery of infringing products.

items.title: Christian Louboutin SAS v. Nakul Bajaj and Others
items.text:
Christian Louboutin SAS v. Nakul Bajaj and Others - Ratio Decidendi: When an e-commerce website crosses the line from being a passive conduit into an active participant by warehousing, quality checking, and promoting counterfeit goods, it incurs direct and contributory liability under Section 79(3) of the IT Act and cannot seek safe harbor immunity.
[Citations: 2018:DHC:7175 | 253 (2018) DLT 728]

items.title: Satyabrata Ghose v. Mugneeram Bangur & Co. and Another
items.text:
Satyabrata Ghose v. Mugneeram Bangur & Co. and Another - Holding 1: Issue: Scope and exhaustiveness of Section 56 Contract Act
Holding: Section 56 of the Indian Contract Act lays down a positive rule of law relating to frustration and does not leave the matter to the intention of the parties or English common law implied term doctrines.

items.title: Satyabrata Ghose v. Mugneeram Bangur & Co. and Another
items.text: Satyabrata Ghose v. Mugneeram Bangur & Co. and Another - Paragraph 16: 16. It must be remembered that 'impossibility' under Section 56 does not mean literal physical impossibility. The performance of an act may not be physically impossible, yet it might be impracticable and useless from the point of view of the object and purpose which the parties had in view; and if an untoward event or change of circumstances upsets the very foundation upon which the parties rested their bargain, it can very well be said that the promisor finds it impossible to do the act which he promised to do.

items.title: Satyabrata Ghose v. Mugneeram Bangur & Co. and Another
items.text: Satyabrata Ghose v. Mugneeram Bangur & Co. and Another - Paragraph 9: 9. The doctrine of frustration is really an aspect or part of the law of discharge of contract by reason of supervening impossibility or illegality of the act agreed to be done and hence comes within the purview of Section 56 of the Indian Contract Act. Section 56 lays down a rule of positive law and does not leave the matter to be determined according to the intention of the parties.

items.title: Satyabrata Ghose v. Mugneeram Bangur & Co. and Another
items.text:
Satyabrata Ghose v. Mugneeram Bangur & Co. and Another - Ratio Decidendi: Section 56 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 is exhaustive as regards the law relating to frustration of contracts in India. The performance of an act may become impossible not only when it is physically impossible, but also when an untoward event or change of circumstances totally upsets the foundation on which the parties rested their bargain. However, temporary requisitioning during war which merely causes delay does not dissolve the contract where time is not of the essence.
[Citations: (1954) SCR 310 | AIR 1954 SC 44]

items.title: Kesavananda Bharati Sripadagalvaru v. State of Kerala
items.text:
Kesavananda Bharati Sripadagalvaru v. State of Kerala - Holding 1: Issue: Limits on parliamentary amending power under Article 368
Holding: Article 368 does not enable Parliament to alter the basic structure or framework of the Constitution.

items.title: Kesavananda Bharati Sripadagalvaru v. State of Kerala
items.text: Kesavananda Bharati Sripadagalvaru v. State of Kerala - Paragraph 292: The power to amend under Article 368 does not include the power to alter the basic structure of the Constitution so as to change its identity. Supremacy of the Constitution, republican and democratic form of government, secular character, separation of powers, and federal character are elements of the basic structure.

items.title: Kesavananda Bharati Sripadagalvaru v. State of Kerala
items.text:
Kesavananda Bharati Sripadagalvaru v. State of Kerala - Ratio Decidendi: Parliament has the power to amend any part of the Constitution under Article 368, but this power is not unlimited and does not extend to abrogating or destroying the basic structure or essential framework of the Constitution.
[Citations: (1973) 4 SCC 225 | 1973 INSC 258 | AIR 1973 SC 1461]

items.title: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India
items.text:
Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India - Holding 1: Issue: Is the right to travel abroad protected under Article 21?
Holding: The expression 'personal liberty' in Article 21 is of the widest amplitude and encompasses the right to travel abroad. No person can be deprived of this right except according to procedure established by law.

items.title: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India
items.text:
Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India - Holding 2: Issue: Does procedure under Article 21 require fairness and natural justice?
Holding: The procedure established by law under Article 21 must not be arbitrary, fanciful or oppressive; it must be just, fair and reasonable, embodying the principles of natural justice.

items.title: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India
items.text: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India - Paragraph 5: The expression 'personal liberty' in Article 21 is of the widest amplitude and it covers a variety of rights which go to constitute the personal liberty of man, including the right to travel abroad.

items.title: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India
items.text: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India - Paragraph 7: The procedure contemplated by Article 21 must be 'right and just and fair' and not arbitrary, fanciful or oppressive; otherwise, it'd be no procedure at all and the requirement of Article 21 would not be satisfied.

items.title: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India
items.text: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India - Ratio Decidendi: In Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India, WP (Civil) No. 231 of 1977, the procedural journey commenced with admission notice and Rule nisi issued on 1977-07-18, culminating in the 7-Judge Constitution Bench judgment delivered on 1978-01-25. The Supreme Court held that the procedure contemplated by Article 21 must be right, just, and fair, and not arbitrary. Article 14, Article 19, and Article 21 form an interlinked Golden Triangle of fundamental rights: any law depriving personal liberty must stand the test of Article 14 (equality and non-arbitrariness), Article 19 (fundamental freedoms), and Article 21.

items.title: D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal
items.text:
D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal - Holding 1: Issue: Mandatory guidelines on arrest and detention
Holding: The Supreme Court laid down 11 mandatory requirements to be followed in all cases of arrest and detention until statutory provisions are enacted.

items.title: D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal
items.text: D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal - Paragraph 35: The police personnel carrying out the arrest and handling the interrogation of the arrestee should bear accurate, visible and clear identification and name tags with their designations. A memo of arrest shall be prepared at the time of arrest and attested by at least one witness.

items.title: D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal
items.text:
D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal - Ratio Decidendi: Custodial violence, torture and death in custody strike at the rule of law and Article 21. Police personnel making arrests must prepare an arrest memo, inform relatives within 8-12 hours, and ensure medical examination every 48 hours.
[Citations: (1997) 1 SCC 416 | 1996 INSC 1579 | AIR 1997 SC 610]

items.title: Jacob Mathew v. State of Punjab and Another
items.text:
Jacob Mathew v. State of Punjab and Another - Holding 1: Issue: Standard of medical negligence in criminal law
Holding: Simple lack of care, an error of judgment, or an accident is not proof of criminal negligence on the part of a medical professional. Gross negligence must be demonstrated beyond reasonable doubt.

items.title: Jacob Mathew v. State of Punjab and Another
items.text: Jacob Mathew v. State of Punjab and Another - Paragraph 48: A medical practitioner cannot be held liable for criminal negligence simply because a better alternative course of treatment was available or because patient did not respond favorably. Criminal liability requires gross negligence.

items.title: Jacob Mathew v. State of Punjab and Another
items.text: Jacob Mathew v. State of Punjab and Another - Ratio Decidendi: In Jacob Mathew v. State of Punjab (2005) 6 SCC 1, the Supreme Court held that to prosecute a medical professional under penal law (Section 304A IPC / Section 106 BNS), the negligence must be gross, reckless, or of such high degree as to indicate disregard for human life, adopting the Bolam test standard. Simple lack of care or an error of judgment does not constitute criminal negligence. Investigating officers should obtain an independent medical opinion before proceeding with criminal arrest.

items.title: Satyawati Sharma (Dead) by LRs v. Union of India and Another
items.text:
Satyawati Sharma (Dead) by LRs v. Union of India and Another - Holding 1: Issue: Constitutional validity of Section 14(1)(e) DRC Act confining bona fide eviction to residential premises
Holding: The discriminatory classification between residential and commercial premises under Section 14(1)(e) DRC Act is unconstitutional and severed. Landlords can seek eviction for bona fide requirement for commercial premises as well.

items.title: Satyawati Sharma (Dead) by LRs v. Union of India and Another
items.text: Satyawati Sharma (Dead) by LRs v. Union of India and Another - Paragraph 38: 38. Section 14(1)(e) of the 1958 Act is violative of the doctrine of equality embodied in Article 14 of the Constitution of India insofar as it discriminates between the premises let for residential and non-residential purposes when the same are required bona fide by the landlord for occupation for himself or for any member of his family dependent on him.

items.title: Satyawati Sharma (Dead) by LRs v. Union of India and Another
items.text: Satyawati Sharma (Dead) by LRs v. Union of India and Another - Paragraph 41: 41. By striking down the discriminatory portion, Section 14(1)(e) will now read: 'that the premises are required bona fide by the landlord for occupation as a residence for himself or for any member of his family dependent on him, if he is the owner thereof, or for any person for whose benefit the premises are held and that the landlord or such person has no other reasonably suitable accommodation'.

items.title: Satyawati Sharma (Dead) by LRs v. Union of India and Another
items.text:
Satyawati Sharma (Dead) by LRs v. Union of India and Another - Ratio Decidendi: Section 14(1)(e) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, violates Article 14 of the Constitution to the extent that it discriminates between premises let for residential and non-residential purposes by restricting the landlord's right to seek eviction on the ground of bona fide requirement only to residential premises. The words 'let for residential purposes' are severed, enabling landlords to seek eviction for commercial bona fide requirement.
[Citations: (2008) 5 SCC 287 | AIR 2008 SC 3148]

items.title: Rangappa v. Sri Mohan
items.text:
Rangappa v. Sri Mohan - Holding 1: Issue: Does Section 139 presumption extend to existence of legally enforceable debt?
Holding: The presumption mandated by Section 139 does indeed include the existence of a legally enforceable debt or liability. Observations in Krishna Janardhan Bhat (2008) 4 SCC 54 to the contrary do not state the correct position of law and are overruled.

items.title: Rangappa v. Sri Mohan
items.text:
Rangappa v. Sri Mohan - Holding 2: Issue: Standard of proof for accused to rebut Section 139 presumption
Holding: The standard of proof for rebutting the presumption under Section 139 is that of preponderance of probabilities. The accused is not required to prove his defence beyond reasonable doubt and can rely on the materials adduced by the complainant.

items.title: Rangappa v. Sri Mohan
items.text: Rangappa v. Sri Mohan - Paragraph 26: 26. In light of these extracts, we are in agreement with the respondent-claimant that the presumption mandated by Section 139 of the Act does indeed include the existence of a legally enforceable debt or liability. To that extent, the dictum in Krishna Janardhan Bhat (2008) 4 SCC 54 may not be correct. However, this does not mean that the drawer of the cheque is without a defence.

items.title: Rangappa v. Sri Mohan
items.text: Rangappa v. Sri Mohan - Paragraph 27: 27. Section 139 of the Act is an example of a reverse onus clause that has been included in furtherance of the legislative objective of improving the credibility of negotiable instruments. While Section 138 of the Act specifies a strong criminal remedy in relation to the dishonour of cheques, the rebuttable presumption under Section 139 is a device to prevent undue delay in the course of litigation. However, it must be remembered that the offence made punishable by Section 138 can be better described as a regulatory offence.

items.title: Rangappa v. Sri Mohan
items.text: Rangappa v. Sri Mohan - Paragraph 28: 28. It is a well-settled principle of law that in criminal cases, while the prosecution must prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt, the accused who wishes to establish a defence or rebut a statutory presumption is only required to satisfy the test of preponderance of probabilities. The accused can rely on the materials submitted by the complainant in order to raise such a defence and it is conceivable that in some cases the accused may not need to adduce evidence of his/her own.

items.title: Rangappa v. Sri Mohan
items.text:
Rangappa v. Sri Mohan - Ratio Decidendi: The presumption mandated by Section 139 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 includes the existence of a legally enforceable debt or liability. However, this presumption is rebuttable, and the standard of proof required from the accused is that of a preponderance of probabilities. The observations to the contrary in Krishna Janardhan Bhat (2008) 4 SCC 54 stand overruled.
[Citations: (2010) 11 SCC 441 | 2010 INSC 355 | AIR 2010 SC 1898]

items.title: Anvar P.V. v. P.K. Basheer and Others
items.text:
Anvar P.V. v. P.K. Basheer and Others - Holding 1: Issue: Admissibility of secondary electronic evidence outside Section 65B
Holding: Sections 63 and 65 of the Evidence Act have no application in the case of secondary evidence by way of electronic record; the same is wholly governed by Sections 65A and 65B. Generalia specialibus non derogant.

items.title: Anvar P.V. v. P.K. Basheer and Others
items.text: Anvar P.V. v. P.K. Basheer and Others - Paragraph 14: 14. Any documentary evidence by way of an electronic record under the Evidence Act, in view of Sections 59 and 65A, can be proved only in accordance with the procedure prescribed under Section 65B. Section 65A of the Evidence Act creates a special law for electronic records. The situation is governed by the special provisions Section 65A and Section 65B. These sections are a complete code in themselves.

items.title: Anvar P.V. v. P.K. Basheer and Others
items.text: Anvar P.V. v. P.K. Basheer and Others - Paragraph 16: 16. Most importantly, Section 65B begins with a non-obstante clause: 'Notwithstanding anything contained in this Act...'. Therefore, the special law under Section 65B overrides the general law on secondary evidence under Sections 63 and 65 of the Evidence Act.

items.title: Anvar P.V. v. P.K. Basheer and Others
items.text: Anvar P.V. v. P.K. Basheer and Others - Paragraph 22: 22. The judgment of this Court in State (NCT of Delhi) v. Navjot Sandhu (2005) 11 SCC 600, to the extent it holds that irrespective of the compliance with Section 65B, electronic evidence can be proved under Sections 63 and 65, does not lay down the correct legal position and is overruled.

items.title: Anvar P.V. v. P.K. Basheer and Others
items.text:
Anvar P.V. v. P.K. Basheer and Others - Ratio Decidendi: An electronic record by way of secondary evidence shall not be admitted in evidence unless the requirements under Section 65B are satisfied. The Evidence Act does not contemplate or permit the proof of an electronic record by oral evidence if the requirements under Section 65B of the Act are not complied with. State (NCT of Delhi) v. Navjot Sandhu overruled to the extent it held electronic records could be proved under Section 63 and 65.
[Citations: (2014) 10 SCC 473 | 2014 INSC 650 | AIR 2015 SC 180]

items.title: Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar and Another
items.text:
Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar and Another - Holding 1: Issue: Restraints on arrest for offences up to seven years
Holding: Police officers shall not automatically arrest accused persons when an offence is punishable with imprisonment up to seven years without satisfying parameters of Section 41 CrPC (Section 35 BNSS).

items.title: Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar and Another
items.text: Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar and Another - Paragraph 11: No arrest should be made merely because the offence is non-bailable and cognizable. The police officer must be satisfied that arrest is necessary to prevent further offence, for proper investigation, or to prevent tampering with evidence.

items.title: Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar and Another
items.text:
Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar and Another - Ratio Decidendi: Arrest should not be made automatically upon registration of a case. For offences punishable with imprisonment for a term up to seven years, police officers must serve notice of appearance under Section 41A CrPC (Section 35(3) BNSS) and record reasons for arrest in writing.
[Citations: (2014) 8 SCC 273 | 2014 INSC 485 | AIR 2014 SC 2756]

items.title: Lalita Kumari v. Government of Uttar Pradesh and Others
items.text:
Lalita Kumari v. Government of Uttar Pradesh and Others - Holding 1: Issue: Mandatory registration of FIR under Section 154
Holding: Registration of FIR is mandatory under Section 154 of the Code if the information discloses commission of a cognizable offence and no preliminary inquiry is permissible in such a situation.

items.title: Lalita Kumari v. Government of Uttar Pradesh and Others
items.text: Lalita Kumari v. Government of Uttar Pradesh and Others - Paragraph 120: Registration of FIR is mandatory under Section 154 of the Code, if the information discloses commission of a cognizable offence and no preliminary inquiry is permissible in such a situation. Preliminary inquiry may be conducted only in matrimonial, commercial, medical negligence, or corruption cases.

items.title: Lalita Kumari v. Government of Uttar Pradesh and Others
items.text:
Lalita Kumari v. Government of Uttar Pradesh and Others - Ratio Decidendi: Section 154 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Section 173 BNSS 2023) is mandatory. If information discloses a cognizable offence, the police officer must register an FIR without conducting preliminary inquiry.
[Citations: (2014) 2 SCC 1 | 2013 INSC 792 | AIR 2014 SC 187]

items.title: Shreya Singhal v. Union of India
items.text:
Shreya Singhal v. Union of India - Holding 1: Issue: Constitutionality of Section 66A IT Act
Holding: Section 66A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 is struck down in its entirety being violative of Article 19(1)(a) and not saved by Article 19(2).

items.title: Shreya Singhal v. Union of India
items.text: Shreya Singhal v. Union of India - Paragraph 119: Section 66A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 is struck down in its entirety being violative of Article 19(1)(a) and not saved by Article 19(2). It is vague and has a chilling effect on speech.

items.title: Shreya Singhal v. Union of India
items.text:
Shreya Singhal v. Union of India - Ratio Decidendi: Section 66A of the Information Technology Act is unconstitutionally vague and overbroad, penalizing discussion and advocacy rather than incitement. It chills free speech on the internet and fails to satisfy Article 19(2) reasonableness.
[Citations: (2015) 5 SCC 1 | 2015 INSC 249 | AIR 2015 SC 1523]

items.title: Energy Watchdog v. Central Electricity Regulatory Commission and Others
items.text:
Energy Watchdog v. Central Electricity Regulatory Commission and Others - Holding 1: Issue: Commercial unviability vs Frustration
Holding: Mere commercial difficulty or price escalation does not constitute frustration of contract under Section 56 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872.

items.title: Energy Watchdog v. Central Electricity Regulatory Commission and Others
items.text: Energy Watchdog v. Central Electricity Regulatory Commission and Others - Paragraph 37: The doctrine of frustration cannot be availed of by a party simply because performance has become more onerous or expensive. Section 56 of the Contract Act does not apply to commercial hardship.

items.title: Energy Watchdog v. Central Electricity Regulatory Commission and Others
items.text:
Energy Watchdog v. Central Electricity Regulatory Commission and Others - Ratio Decidendi: Section 56 of the Contract Act applies only when an untoward event or change of circumstance totally upsets the very foundation of the contract. An increase in cost or commercial unviability does not discharge a party from contractual performance.
[Citations: (2017) 14 SCC 80 | 2017 INSC 338]

items.title: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India (2017) 10 SCC 1
items.text: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India (2017) 10 SCC 1 - Paragraph 1: The reference to the nine Judge Bench arises out of a challenge to the constitutional validity of the Aadhaar card scheme. The petitioners contend that the scheme infringes the fundamental right to privacy guaranteed by Part III of the Constitution.

items.title: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India (2017) 10 SCC 1
items.text: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India (2017) 10 SCC 1 - Paragraph 2: In M.P. Sharma v. Satish Chandra, District Magistrate, Delhi (1954) SCR 1077 and Kharak Singh v. State of U.P. (1964) 1 SCR 332, observations were made by benches of eight and six Judges respectively to the effect that the Constitution does not specifically protect a right to privacy.

items.title: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India (2017) 10 SCC 1
items.text: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India (2017) 10 SCC 1 - Paragraph 3: The question which falls for determination before this Bench is whether the right to privacy is a fundamental right guaranteed under Part III of the Constitution of India.

items.title: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India (2017) 10 SCC 1
items.text: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India (2017) 10 SCC 1 - Paragraph 4: Privacy is a constitutionally protected right which emerges, primarily, from the guarantee of life and personal liberty in Article 21 of the Constitution. Elements of privacy also arise in varying contexts from the other facets of freedom and dignity recognised and guaranteed by the fundamental rights contained in Part III.

items.title: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India (2017) 10 SCC 1
items.text: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India (2017) 10 SCC 1 - Paragraph 5: RATIO DECIDENDI: The right to privacy is protected as an intrinsic part of the right to life and personal liberty under Article 21 and as a part of the freedoms guaranteed by Part III of the Constitution. The decisions in M.P. Sharma and Kharak Singh to the extent they hold that privacy is not a fundamental right stand overruled.

items.title: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India (2017) 10 SCC 1
items.text: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India (2017) 10 SCC 1 - Paragraph 6: JUDGMENT

items.title: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India (2017) 10 SCC 1
items.text: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India (2017) 10 SCC 1 - Ratio Decidendi: The right to privacy is protected as an intrinsic part of the right to life and personal liberty under Article 21 and as a part of the freedoms guaranteed by Part III of the Constitution. The decisions in M.P. Sharma and Kharak Singh to the extent they hold that privacy is not a fundamental right stand overruled.

items.title: Shafhi Mohammad v. State of Himachal Pradesh
items.text:
Shafhi Mohammad v. State of Himachal Pradesh - Holding 1: Issue: Exemption from Section 65B certificate
Holding: Requirement of producing certificate under Section 65B(4) is not always mandatory and can be relaxed whenever interest of justice so warrants, particularly where party is not in possession of the device.

items.title: Shafhi Mohammad v. State of Himachal Pradesh
items.text: Shafhi Mohammad v. State of Himachal Pradesh - Paragraph 11: 11. Accordingly, we clarify the legal position on the subject to the effect that the requirement of certificate under Section 65B(4) is not always mandatory. Where the electronic record is produced by a party who is not in possession of a device, Sections 63 and 65 of the Evidence Act can be applied and the certificate requirement can be dispensed with.

items.title: Shafhi Mohammad v. State of Himachal Pradesh
items.text:
Shafhi Mohammad v. State of Himachal Pradesh - Ratio Decidendi: Held that Section 65B certificate is not mandatory if the party producing secondary evidence is not in possession of the device. (Note: Expressly overruled in Arjun Panditrao Khotkar (2020) 7 SCC 1).
[Citations: (2018) 2 SCC 801 | 2018 INSC 92]

items.title: Perkins Eastman Architects DPC and Another v. HSCC (India) Ltd.
items.text:
Perkins Eastman Architects DPC and Another v. HSCC (India) Ltd. - Holding 1: Issue: Unilateral appointment of sole arbitrator by interested entity
Holding: A person who has an interest in the outcome or decision of the dispute cannot be permitted to nominate or appoint a sole arbitrator to resolve such dispute. TRF Ltd. extended.

items.title: Perkins Eastman Architects DPC and Another v. HSCC (India) Ltd.
items.text: Perkins Eastman Architects DPC and Another v. HSCC (India) Ltd. - Paragraph 16: 16. In TRF Limited v. Energo Engineering Projects Ltd. (2017) 8 SCC 377, the question was whether the Managing Director, who became ineligible by operation of Section 12(5) read with Seventh Schedule, could nominate an arbitrator. This Court held that once the Managing Director became ineligible, he could not nominate an arbitrator.

items.title: Perkins Eastman Architects DPC and Another v. HSCC (India) Ltd.
items.text: Perkins Eastman Architects DPC and Another v. HSCC (India) Ltd. - Paragraph 21: 21. The ineligibility contemplated by Section 12(5) must also extend to the nomination of a sole arbitrator by a person having an interest in the dispute. If a person has an interest in the outcome or decision of the dispute, they must not have the power to appoint a sole arbitrator, for whatever advantage a party may derive by nominating an arbitrator of their choice would definitely run counter to fairness and equality.

items.title: Perkins Eastman Architects DPC and Another v. HSCC (India) Ltd.
items.text:
Perkins Eastman Architects DPC and Another v. HSCC (India) Ltd. - Ratio Decidendi: A person who is ineligible to act as an arbitrator under Section 12(5) read with the Seventh Schedule of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, is equally disqualified from unilaterally appointing a sole arbitrator. Independence and impartiality are the hallmark of any arbitration proceedings, and counterparty unilateral control over the tribunal constitution vitiates the arbitral process.
[Citations: (2020) 20 SCC 760 | 2019 INSC 1289 | AIR 2020 SC 59]

items.title: Sushila Aggarwal and Others v. State (NCT of Delhi) and Another
items.text:
Sushila Aggarwal and Others v. State (NCT of Delhi) and Another - Holding 1: Issue: Duration of anticipatory bail
Holding: Protection granted under Section 438 CrPC / Section 482 BNSS should not be limited to a fixed period; it ordinarily continues till the end of the trial unless special circumstances warrant limitation.

items.title: Sushila Aggarwal and Others v. State (NCT of Delhi) and Another
items.text: Sushila Aggarwal and Others v. State (NCT of Delhi) and Another - Paragraph 91: The protection granted to a person under Section 438 CrPC should not invariably be limited to a fixed period; it should inure in favour of the accused without any restriction on time till the end of the trial.

items.title: Sushila Aggarwal and Others v. State (NCT of Delhi) and Another
items.text:
Sushila Aggarwal and Others v. State (NCT of Delhi) and Another - Ratio Decidendi: Anticipatory bail under Section 438 CrPC (Section 482 BNSS) need not be restricted in duration or capped until the filing of charge sheet. The Constitution Bench reaffirmed the law in Gurbaksh Singh Sibbia, emphasizing that personal liberty under Article 21 cannot be unnecessarily truncated.
[Citations: (2020) 5 SCC 1 | 2020 INSC 106 | AIR 2020 SC 831]

items.title: Vidya Drolia and Others v. Durga Trading Corporation
items.text:
Vidya Drolia and Others v. Durga Trading Corporation - Holding 1: Issue: Fourfold test of arbitrability
Holding: The Supreme Court propounded a fourfold test of non-arbitrability: actions in rem, disputes affecting third-party rights, inalienable sovereign functions, and matters expressly reserved by statute for special courts.

items.title: Vidya Drolia and Others v. Durga Trading Corporation
items.text:
Vidya Drolia and Others v. Durga Trading Corporation - Holding 2: Issue: Arbitrability of landlord-tenant disputes
Holding: Landlord-tenant disputes under the Transfer of Property Act are arbitrable as they are actions in personam; only tenancy disputes covered by special rent control legislation are non-arbitrable.

items.title: Vidya Drolia and Others v. Durga Trading Corporation
items.text: Vidya Drolia and Others v. Durga Trading Corporation - Paragraph 76: Disputes are not arbitrable when the cause of action relates to actions in rem, affects third party rights, pertains to sovereign functions of the State, or is expressly or impliedly non-arbitrable under mandatory statutory provisions.

items.title: Vidya Drolia and Others v. Durga Trading Corporation
items.text:
Vidya Drolia and Others v. Durga Trading Corporation - Ratio Decidendi: Landlord-tenant disputes governed by the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 are arbitrable. Himangni Enterprises v. Kamaljeet Singh Ahluwalia (2017) 10 SCC 706 is overruled.
[Citations: (2021) 2 SCC 1 | 2020 INSC 697 | AIR 2021 SC 79]

items.title: Satender Kumar Antil v. Central Bureau of Investigation and Another
items.text:
Satender Kumar Antil v. Central Bureau of Investigation and Another - Holding 1: Issue: Bail principles and arrest compliance
Holding: Bail is the rule and jail is the exception. Non-compliance with Section 41 and 41A CrPC (Section 35 BNSS 2023) entitles the accused to bail as of right.

items.title: Satender Kumar Antil v. Central Bureau of Investigation and Another
items.text: Satender Kumar Antil v. Central Bureau of Investigation and Another - Paragraph 100: 100. Category A offences (punishable with imprisonment of 7 years or less) require that after filing of chargesheet, summons should ordinarily be issued in the first instance. If the accused was not arrested during investigation, bail application may be decided without insisting upon custodial detention.

items.title: Satender Kumar Antil v. Central Bureau of Investigation and Another
items.text: Satender Kumar Antil v. Central Bureau of Investigation and Another - Paragraph 26: 26. Section 41 and 41A of the Code are salutary provisions and compliance thereof is mandatory. A court, while considering the application for custody or remand under Section 167 of the Code, is duty-bound to satisfy itself that the mandate of Section 41 and 41A has been strictly adhered to. Any arrest made in violation of the mandate under Section 41 and 41A will entitle the accused to grant of bail.

items.title: Satender Kumar Antil v. Central Bureau of Investigation and Another
items.text: Satender Kumar Antil v. Central Bureau of Investigation and Another - Paragraph 73: 73. The principle that bail is the rule and jail is the exception has been repeated time and again by this Court. Personal liberty is a very precious fundamental right guaranteed under Article 21 of the Constitution. Deprivation of liberty even for a single day is one day too many.

items.title: Satender Kumar Antil v. Central Bureau of Investigation and Another
items.text:
Satender Kumar Antil v. Central Bureau of Investigation and Another - Ratio Decidendi: Arrest is a draconian power that cannot be exercised mechanically. When an accused person is not arrested during investigation and cooperates with the police pursuant to notice under Section 41A CrPC (Section 35(3) BNSS 2023), the court upon filing of chargesheet shall not mechanically remand the accused to judicial custody but decide bail applications on the same day or without custodial remand.
[Citations: (2022) 10 SCC 51 | 2022 INSC 690 | AIR 2022 SC 3386]

items.title: In Re: Interplay Between Arbitration Agreements under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 and the Indian Stamp Act, 1899
items.text:
In Re: Interplay Between Arbitration Agreements under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 and the Indian Stamp Act, 1899 - Holding 1: Issue: Effect of non-stamping of underlying contract on arbitration agreement at referral stage
Holding: Non-stamping or insufficient stamping of the underlying contract is a curable defect under the Stamp Act. It does not render the arbitration agreement void ab initio or non-existent. Under Section 16 (competence-competence), the Arbitral Tribunal possesses primary jurisdiction to examine stamping issues.

items.title: In Re: Interplay Between Arbitration Agreements under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 and the Indian Stamp Act, 1899
items.text:
In Re: Interplay Between Arbitration Agreements under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 and the Indian Stamp Act, 1899 - Holding 2: Issue: Correctness of NN Global 5-Judge Bench judgment
Holding: The view taken in NN Global (2023) 7 SCC 1 and SMS Tea Estates (2011) 14 SCC 66 that an unstamped contract cannot be acted upon by the referral court under Section 11 is overruled.

items.title: In Re: Interplay Between Arbitration Agreements under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 and the Indian Stamp Act, 1899
items.text: In Re: Interplay Between Arbitration Agreements under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 and the Indian Stamp Act, 1899 - Paragraph 162: 162. The deficiency in stamping is a curable defect. The Indian Stamp Act, 1899 itself provides a procedure for the payment of requisite stamp duty along with penalty, upon which the instrument is validated and rendered admissible in evidence. Therefore, an unstamped instrument is not void ab initio; it is merely inadmissible until stamped in accordance with law.

items.title: In Re: Interplay Between Arbitration Agreements under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 and the Indian Stamp Act, 1899
items.text: In Re: Interplay Between Arbitration Agreements under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 and the Indian Stamp Act, 1899 - Paragraph 175: 175. The principle of competence-competence, enshrined in Section 16 of the Arbitration Act, empowers the arbitral tribunal to rule on its own jurisdiction, including ruling on any objections with respect to the existence or validity of the arbitration agreement. Harmonious construction dictates that the court at the referral stage under Section 11(6) must confine its examination to the prima facie existence of the arbitration agreement.

items.title: In Re: Interplay Between Arbitration Agreements under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 and the Indian Stamp Act, 1899
items.text: In Re: Interplay Between Arbitration Agreements under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 and the Indian Stamp Act, 1899 - Paragraph 224: 224. In view of the above discussion, we hold that: (a) Unstamped or insufficiently stamped agreements are not void or invalid; (b) Non-stamping is a curable defect; (c) Objections as to stamping fall within the domain of the arbitral tribunal under Section 16; and (d) The decision in NN Global (2023) 7 SCC 1 and SMS Tea Estates (2011) 14 SCC 66 stand overruled.

items.title: In Re: Interplay Between Arbitration Agreements under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 and the Indian Stamp Act, 1899
items.text:
In Re: Interplay Between Arbitration Agreements under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 and the Indian Stamp Act, 1899 - Ratio Decidendi: An unstamped or insufficiently stamped underlying agreement is inadmissible in evidence under Section 35 of the Stamp Act, but this is a curable defect and does not render the arbitration clause void, non-existent, or invalid. At the referral stage under Section 8 or Section 11 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, the court must only examine the prima facie existence of the arbitration agreement, leaving questions of stamping and admissibility to the arbitral tribunal under Section 16.
[Citations: (2024) 6 SCC 1 | 2023 INSC 1066]

items.title: The Maharashtra Police Act, 1951
The Maharashtra Police Act, 1951
The Maharashtra Police Act, 1951
items.text: The Maharashtra Police Act, 1951 - Section 57: 57. Removal of persons convicted of certain offences.—If a person has been convicted of an offence under Chapter XII, XVI or XVII of the Indian Penal Code, or of an offence under section 4 or 12A of the Bombay Prevention of Gambling Act, 1887, or under the Prohibition Act, the Commissioner, the District Magistrate or the Sub-Divisional Magistrate may, if he has reason to believe that such person is likely again to engage in the commission of an offence similar to that for which he was convicted, direct such person to remove himself outside the area specified in the order.

items.title: The Maharashtra Rent Control Act, 1999
items.text:
The Maharashtra Rent Control Act, 1999 - Section 15: 15. No ejectment ordinarily to be made if tenant pays or is ready and willing to pay standard rent and permitted increases.—
(1) A landlord shall not be entitled to the recovery of possession of any premises so long as the tenant pays, or is ready and willing to pay, the amount of the standard rent and permitted increases, if any, and observes and performs the other conditions of the tenancy, in so far as they are consistent with the provisions of this Act.
(2) No suit for recovery of possession shall be instituted by a landlord against a tenant on the ground of non-payment of the standard rent or permitted increases, until the expiration of ninety days next after notice in writing of the demand of the standard rent or permitted increases has been served upon the tenant in the manner provided in section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882.
(3) No decree for eviction shall be passed by the court in any suit for recovery of possession on the ground of arrears of standard rent and permitted increases if, within a period of ninety days from the date of service of the summons of the suit, the tenant pays or tenders in court the standard rent and permitted increases then due.

items.title: The Maharashtra Rent Control Act, 1999
The Maharashtra Rent Control Act, 1999
items.text:
The Maharashtra Rent Control Act, 1999 - Section 24: 24. Landlord entitled to recover possession of premises given on licence on expiry.—
(1) Notwithstanding anything contained in this Act, a licensee in possession or occupation of premises given to him on licence for residence shall deliver possession of such premises to the landlord on expiry of the period of licence; and on the failure of the licensee to so deliver the possession of the licensed premises, a landlord shall be entitled to recover possession of such premises from a licensee, on the expiry of the period of licence, by making an application to the Competent Authority, and the Competent Authority, on being satisfied that the period of licence has expired, shall pass an order for eviction of a licensee.
(2) Any licensee who does not deliver possession of the premises to the landlord on expiry of the period of licence and continues to be in possession or occupation of the licensed premises shall be liable to pay damages at double the rate of the licence fee or charge of the premises fixed under the agreement of licence.

Commencement Notification for Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (S.O. 849(E))
items.text:
Commencement Notification for Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (S.O. 849(E)) - Section Notification S.O. 849(E): MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS NOTIFICATION, New Delhi, the 23rd February, 2024.
S.O. 849(E).—In exercise of the powers conferred by sub-section (2) of section 1 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (45 of 2023), the Central Government hereby appoints the 1st day of July, 2024 as the date on which the provisions of the said Sanhita, except the provisions of sub-section (2) of section 106, shall come into force. The operation of Section 106(2) regarding hit-and-run accidents is deferred.

Temporal Applicability and Savings:
For any crime or offence committed prior to 1 July 2024 (e.g. 15 January 2024), by virtue of Article 20(1) of the Constitution of India and Section 531(2)(a) of the BNSS, the substantive penal law applicable remains the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (such as Section 302 IPC for murder). BNS 2023 cannot be applied retrospectively.

items.title: Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020
items.text:
Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020 - Section Rule 4: Rule 4. Duties of e-commerce entities.—(1) An e-commerce entity shall be a company incorporated under the Companies Act, 1956 or the Companies Act, 2013 or a foreign company or an office, branch or agency outside India owned or controlled by a person resident in India.
(2) Appoint a nodal person of contact or an alternate senior designated functionary who is resident in India, to ensure compliance with the provisions of the Act or the rules made thereunder.
(3) Every e-commerce entity shall provide in a clear and accessible manner on its platform the legal name of the entity, principal geographic address of its headquarters and all branches, name and details of its website, and contact details including email address, fax, and telephone numbers.
(4) Every e-commerce entity shall establish an adequate grievance redressal mechanism and appoint a grievance officer for consumer grievance redressal, and display prominently on its platform the name, designation and contact details of such officer.
(5) The grievance officer shall acknowledge receipt of any consumer complaint within forty-eight hours and redress the complaint within one month from the date of receipt of the complaint.

items.title: Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020
items.text:
Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020 - Section Rule 5: Rule 5. Marketplace e-commerce entities.—(1) A marketplace e-commerce entity shall require sellers through an undertaking to ensure that descriptions, images, and other content pertaining to goods or services on their platform are accurate and correspond directly with the appearance, nature, quality, purpose and other general features of such good or service.
(2) Every marketplace e-commerce entity shall display prominently to its users: details about the sellers offering goods and services, including the name of their business, whether registered or not, their geographic address, customer care number, rating or feedback, and any other information necessary for enabling consumers to make informed decisions at the pre-purchase stage.
(3) No marketplace e-commerce entity shall manipulate the search results or listings in a manner that favors a particular seller or group of sellers.

items.title: Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021
Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021
items.text:
Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 - Section Rule 4: Rule 4. Additional due diligence observed by significant social media intermediary.—(1) A significant social media intermediary shall appoint a Chief Compliance Officer who shall be responsible for ensuring that the intermediary is in compliance with the Act and these rules.
(2) A significant social media intermediary shall appoint a nodal contact person for 24x7 coordination with law enforcement agencies and officers.
(3) A significant social media intermediary shall appoint a Resident Grievance Officer, who shall be an employee and a resident of India.
(4) A significant social media intermediary providing services primarily in the nature of messaging shall enable the identification of the first originator of the information on its computer resource as may be required by a judicial order passed by a court of competent jurisdiction or an order under section 69 by the Competent Authority.

items.title: Information Technology (Reasonable Security Practices and Procedures and Sensitive Personal Data or Information) Rules, 2011
Information Technology (Reasonable Security Practices and Procedures and Sensitive Personal Data or Information) Rules, 2011
Information Technology (Reasonable Security Practices and Procedures and Sensitive Personal Data or Information) Rules, 2011
items.text:
Information Technology (Reasonable Security Practices and Procedures and Sensitive Personal Data or Information) Rules, 2011 - Section Rule 5: Rule 5. Consent and collection standards.—(1) Body corporate or any person on its behalf shall obtain consent, whether in writing or through electronic means, from the provider of the sensitive personal data or information regarding purpose of usage before collection of such information.
(2) Body corporate or any person on its behalf shall not collect sensitive personal data or information unless the information is collected for a lawful purpose connected with a function or activity of the body corporate or any person on its behalf, and the collection of the sensitive personal data or information is considered necessary for that purpose.
(3) While collecting information directly from the person concerned, the body corporate or any person on its behalf shall take such steps as are, in the circumstances, reasonable to ensure that the person concerned is having the knowledge of the fact that the information is being collected, the purpose for which the information is being collected, and the intended recipients of the information.

items.title: Information Technology (Reasonable Security Practices and Procedures and Sensitive Personal Data or Information) Rules, 2011
items.text:
Information Technology (Reasonable Security Practices and Procedures and Sensitive Personal Data or Information) Rules, 2011 - Section Rule 8: Rule 8. Reasonable security practices and procedures.—(1) A body corporate or a person on its behalf shall be considered to have complied with reasonable security practices and procedures, if they have implemented such security practices and standards and have a comprehensive documented information security programme and information security policies that contain managerial, technical, operational and physical security control measures that are commensurate with the information assets being protected with the nature of business.
(2) The international Standard IS/ISO/IEC 27001 on 'Information Technology - Security Techniques - Information Security Management System - Requirements' is one such standard referred to in sub-rule (1).
(3) Any industry association or entity may follow codes of best practices approved and notified by the Central Government.

items.title: The Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996
items.text: The Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 - Section 11: (1) A person of any nationality may be an arbitrator, unless otherwise agreed by the parties. (2) Subject to sub-section (6), the parties are free to agree on a procedure for appointing the arbitrator or arbitrators. (6) Where, under an appointment procedure agreed upon by the parties, a party fails to act as required under that procedure, the appointment shall be made, on an application of the party, by the arbitral institution designated by the Supreme Court, in case of international commercial arbitration, or by the High Court, in case of arbitrations other than international commercial arbitration.

items.title: The Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996
items.text: The Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 - Section 12: (1) When a person is approached in connection with his possible appointment as an arbitrator, he shall disclose in writing any circumstances,— (a) such as the existence either direct or indirect, of any past or present relationship with or interest in any of the parties or in relation to the subject-matter in dispute, whether financial, business, professional or other kind, which is likely to give rise to justifiable doubts as to his independence or impartiality; and (b) which are likely to affect his ability to devote sufficient time to the arbitration and in particular his ability to complete the entire arbitration within a period of twelve months. (5) Notwithstanding any prior agreement to the contrary, any person whose relationship with the parties or counsel falls under any of the categories specified in the Seventh Schedule shall be ineligible to be appointed as an arbitrator.

items.title: The Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996
items.text: The Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 - Section 16: (1) The arbitral tribunal may rule on its own jurisdiction, including ruling on any objections with respect to the existence or validity of the arbitration agreement, and for that purpose,— (a) an arbitration clause which forms part of a contract shall be treated as an agreement independent of the other terms of the contract; and (b) a decision by the arbitral tribunal that the contract is null and void shall not entail ipso jure the invalidity of the arbitration clause (Doctrine of Kompetenz-Kompetenz).

items.title: The Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996
items.text: The Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 - Section 17: (1) A party may, during the arbitral proceedings, apply to the arbitral tribunal— (i) for the appointment of a guardian for a minor or person of unsound mind; (ii) for an interim measure of protection in respect of any of the following matters: (a) the preservation, interim custody or sale of any goods; (b) securing the amount in dispute; (c) the detention, preservation or inspection of any property; (e) such other interim measure of protection as may appear to the arbitral tribunal to be just and convenient. (2) Any order issued by the arbitral tribunal under this section shall be deemed to be an order of the Court for all purposes and shall be enforceable under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908.

items.title: The Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996
items.text: The Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 - Section 29A: (1) The award in matters other than international commercial arbitration shall be made by the arbitral tribunal within a period of twelve months from the date of completion of pleadings under sub-section (4) of section 23. [Inserted by Act 3 of 2016 and amended by Act 33 of 2019].

items.title: The Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996
items.text: The Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 - Section 31: (1) An arbitral award shall be made in writing and shall be signed by the members of the arbitral tribunal. (2) The arbitral award shall state the reasons upon which it is based, unless: (a) the parties have agreed that no reasons are to be given, or (b) the award is an arbitral award on agreed terms under section 30. (7) (a) Unless otherwise agreed by the parties, where and in so far as an arbitral award is for the payment of money, the arbitral tribunal may include in the sum for which the award is made interest, at such rate as it deems reasonable, on the whole or any part of the money.

items.title: The Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996
items.text: The Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 - Section 34: (1) Recourse to a Court against an arbitral award may be made only by an application for setting aside such award in accordance with sub-section (2) and sub-section (3). (2) An arbitral award may be set aside by the Court only if— (b) the Court finds that— (ii) the arbitral award is in conflict with the public policy of India. (2A) An arbitral award arising out of an arbitration other than an international commercial arbitration, may also be set aside by the Court, if the Court finds that the award is vitiated by patent illegality appearing on the face of the award: Provided that an award shall not be set aside merely on the ground of an erroneous application of the law or by reappreciation of evidence.

items.title: The Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996
items.text: The Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 - Section 36: (1) Where the time for making an application to set aside the arbitral award under section 34 has expired, then, subject to the provisions of sub-section (2), such award shall be enforced in accordance with the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 in the same manner as if it were a decree of the court. (2) Where an application to set aside the arbitral award has been filed in the Court under section 34, the filing of such an application shall not by itself render that award unenforceable, unless the Court grants an order of stay of the operation of the said arbitral award in accordance with the provisions of sub-section (3).

items.title: The Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996
items.text: The Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 - Section 37: (1) An appeal shall lie from the following orders (and from no others) to the Court authorized by law to hear appeals from original decrees of the Court passing the order, namely:— (a) refusing to refer the parties to arbitration under section 8; (b) granting or refusing to grant any measure under section 9; (c) setting aside or refusing to set aside an arbitral award under section 34.

items.title: The Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996
items.text: The Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 - Section 7: (1) In this Part, 'arbitration agreement' means an agreement by the parties to submit to arbitration all or certain disputes which have arisen or which may arise between them in respect of a defined legal relationship, whether contractual or not. (2) An arbitration agreement may be in the form of an arbitration clause in a contract or in the form of a separate agreement. (3) An arbitration agreement shall be in writing.

items.title: The Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996
items.text: The Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 - Section 8: (1) A judicial authority, before which an action is brought in a matter which is the subject of an arbitration agreement shall, if a party to the arbitration agreement or any person claiming through or under him, so applies not later than the date of submitting his first statement on the substance of the dispute, refer the parties to arbitration unless it finds that prima facie no valid arbitration agreement exists. [As amended by Act 3 of 2016].

items.title: The Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996
items.text: The Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 - Section 9: (1) A party may, before or during arbitral proceedings or at any time after the making of the arbitral award but before it is enforced in accordance with section 36, apply to a court— (ii) for an interim measure of protection in respect of any of the following matters, namely:— (a) the preservation, interim custody or sale of any goods; (b) securing the amount in dispute in the arbitration; (c) the detention, preservation or inspection of any property... (3) Once the arbitral tribunal has been constituted, the Court shall not entertain an application under sub-section (1), unless the Court finds that circumstances exist which may not render the remedy provided under section 17 efficacious.

items.title: The Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996
items.text: The Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 - Section Seventh Schedule: Seventh Schedule (Section 12(5)): Categories of ineligibility: 1. The arbitrator is an employee, consultant, advisor or has any other past or present business relationship with a party. 2. The arbitrator currently represents or advises one of the parties or an affiliate of one of the parties. 3. The arbitrator has a significant financial or personal interest in one of the parties or the outcome of the dispute. 4. The arbitrator is a close family member of a party or of someone who represents a party.

items.title: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023
items.text: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 - Section 1: (1) This Act may be called the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. (2) It shall come into force on such date as the Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, appoint. (3) Every person shall be liable to punishment under this Sanhita and not otherwise for every act or omission contrary to the provisions thereof, of which he shall be guilty within India.

items.title: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023
items.text: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 - Section 100: Whoever causes death by doing an act with the intention of causing death, or with the intention of causing such bodily injury as is likely to cause death, or with the knowledge that he is likely by such act to cause death, commits the offence of culpable homicide.

items.title: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023
items.text: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 - Section 103: (1) Whoever commits murder shall be punished with death or imprisonment for life, and shall also be liable to fine. (2) When a group of five or more persons acting in concert commits murder on the ground of race, caste or community, sex, place of birth, language, personal belief or any other similar ground, each member of such group shall be punished with death or with imprisonment for life, and shall also be liable to fine.

items.title: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023
items.text: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 - Section 103(1): Whoever commits murder shall be punished with death or imprisonment for life, and shall also be liable to fine.

items.title: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023
items.text: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 - Section 103(2): When a group of five or more persons acting in concert commits murder on the ground of race, caste or community, sex, place of birth, language, personal belief or any other similar ground, each member of such group shall be punished with death or with imprisonment for life, and shall also be liable to fine.

items.title: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023
items.text: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 - Section 109: Whoever does any act with such intention or knowledge, and under such circumstances that, if he by that act caused death, he would be guilty of murder, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine; and if hurt is caused to any person by such act, the offender shall be liable either to imprisonment for life, or to such punishment as is hereinbefore mentioned.

items.title: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023
items.text: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 - Section 111: (1) Any continuing unlawful activity including kidnapping, robbery, vehicle theft, extortion, land grabbing, contract killing, economic offence, cyber-crimes having severe consequences, trafficking in persons, drugs or weapons or illicit goods or services, human trafficking for prostitution or ransom, by any person or a group of persons acting on behalf of an organised crime syndicate shall constitute the offence of organised crime. (2) Whoever commits organised crime shall,— (a) if such offence has resulted in the death of any person, be punished with death or imprisonment for life, and shall also be liable to fine which shall not be less than ten lakh rupees.

items.title: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023
items.text: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 - Section 115: (1) Whoever does any act with the intention of thereby causing hurt to any person, or with the knowledge that he is likely thereby to cause hurt to any person, and does thereby cause hurt to any person, is said 'voluntarily to cause hurt'. (2) Whoever, except in the case provided for by sub-section (1) of section 122, voluntarily causes hurt, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to one year, or with fine which may extend to ten thousand rupees, or with both.

items.title: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023
items.text: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 - Section 117: (1) Whoever voluntarily causes hurt, if the hurt which he intends to cause or knows himself to be likely to cause is grievous hurt, and if the hurt which he causes is grievous hurt, is said 'voluntarily to cause grievous hurt'. (2) Whoever voluntarily causes grievous hurt shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.

items.title: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023
items.text: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 - Section 14: Nothing is an offence which is done by a person who is, or who by reason of a mistake of fact and not by reason of a mistake of law in good faith believes himself to be, bound by law to do it.

items.title: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023
items.text: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 - Section 152: Whoever, purposely or knowingly, by words, either spoken or written, or by signs, or by visible representation, or by electronic communication or by use of financial mean, or otherwise, excites or attempts to excite, secession or armed rebellion or subversive activities, or encourages feelings of separatist activities or endangers sovereignty or unity and integrity of India; or indulges in or commits any such act shall be punished with imprisonment for life or with imprisonment which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.

items.title: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023
items.text: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 - Section 1(1): This Act may be called the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.

items.title: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023
items.text: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 - Section 1(2): It shall come into force on such date as the Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, appoint [Commenced 1 July 2024 via S.O. 849(E)].

items.title: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023
items.text: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 - Section 1(3): Every person shall be liable to punishment under this Sanhita and not otherwise for every act or omission contrary to the provisions thereof, of which he shall be guilty within India.

items.title: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023
items.text: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 - Section 20: Nothing is an offence which is done by a child under seven years of age.

items.title: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023
items.text: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 - Section 22: Nothing is an offence which is done by a person who, at the time of doing it, by reason of unsoundness of mind, is incapable of knowing the nature of the act, or that he is doing what is either wrong or contrary to law.

items.title: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023
items.text: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 - Section 303: (1) Whoever, intending to take dishonestly any movable property out of the possession of any person without that person's consent, moves that property in order to such taking, is said to commit theft. (2) Whoever commits theft shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both.

items.title: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023
items.text: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 - Section 304: (1) Theft is 'snatching' if, in order to commit theft, the offender suddenly or quickly or forcibly seizes, secures, grabs or takes away from any person or from his possession any movable property. (2) Whoever commits snatching shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, and shall also be liable to fine.

items.title: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023
items.text: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 - Section 316: (1) Whoever, being in any manner entrusted with property, or with any dominion over property, dishonestly misappropriates or converts to his own use that property, or dishonestly uses or disposes of that property in violation of any direction of law prescribing the mode in which such trust is to be discharged, commits 'criminal breach of trust'. (2) Whoever commits criminal breach of trust shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to five years, or with fine, or with both.

items.title: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023
items.text: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 - Section 318: (1) Whoever, by deceiving any person, fraudulently or dishonestly induces the person so deceived to deliver any property to any person... is said to 'cheat'. (4) Whoever cheats and thereby dishonestly induces the person deceived to deliver any property... shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.

items.title: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023
items.text: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 - Section 34: Nothing is an offence which is done in the exercise of the right of private defence.

items.title: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023
items.text: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 - Section 35: Every person has a right, subject to the restrictions contained in section 37, to defend— (a) his own body, and the body of any other person, against any offence affecting the human body; (b) the property, whether movable or immovable, of himself or of any other person, against any act which is an offence falling under the definition of theft, robbery, mischief or criminal trespass, or which is an attempt to commit theft, robbery, mischief or criminal trespass.

items.title: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023
items.text: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 - Section 358: (1) The Indian Penal Code is hereby repealed. (2) Notwithstanding the repeal of the Code, the repeal shall not affect— (a) the previous operation of the Code so repealed or anything duly done or suffered thereunder; or (b) any right, privilege, obligation or liability acquired, accrued or incurred under the Code so repealed; or (c) any penalty, forfeiture or punishment incurred in respect of any offence committed against the Code so repealed; or (d) any investigation, legal proceeding or remedy in respect of any such penalty, forfeiture or punishment, and any such investigation, legal proceeding or remedy may be instituted, continued or enforced, and any such penalty, forfeiture or punishment may be imposed as if that Code had not been repealed.

items.title: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023
items.text: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 - Section 358(1): The Indian Penal Code is hereby repealed.

items.title: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023
items.text: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 - Section 358(2): Notwithstanding the repeal of the Code, the repeal shall not affect— (a) the previous operation of the Code so repealed or anything duly done or suffered thereunder; or (b) any right, privilege, obligation or liability acquired, accrued or incurred under the Code so repealed; or (c) any penalty, forfeiture or punishment incurred in respect of any offence committed against the Code so repealed; or (d) any investigation, legal proceeding or remedy in respect of any such penalty, forfeiture or punishment, and any such investigation, legal proceeding or remedy may be instituted, continued or enforced, and any such penalty, forfeiture or punishment may be imposed as if that Code had not been repealed.

items.title: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023
items.text: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 - Section 4: The punishments to which offenders are liable under the provisions of this Sanhita are— (a) Death; (b) Imprisonment for life; (c) Imprisonment, which is of two descriptions, namely:— (1) Rigorous, that is, with hard labour; (2) Simple; (d) Forfeiture of property; (e) Fine; (f) Community service.

items.title: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023
items.text: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 - Section 4 Explanation: Community service shall mean the work which the Court may order a convict to perform as a form of punishment that benefits the community, for which he shall not be entitled to any remuneration.

items.title: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023
items.text: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 - Section 63: A man is said to commit 'rape' if he penetrates his penis, to any extent, into the vagina, mouth, urethra or anus of a woman or makes her to do so with him or any other person... under any of the circumstances falling under the descriptions: against her will, without her consent, or with consent obtained by putting her in fear of death or hurt.
